MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Medical Center
Department of Medical Genetics

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: [redacted name]
DOB: [redacted date]
MRN: [redacted ID]
Specimen Type: Peripheral blood
Collection Date: [redacted date]
Received Date: [redacted date]
Report Date: [redacted date]

REFERRAL REASON
Fragile-X syndrome diagnostic testing

CLINICAL INDICATION
Pediatric patient referred for Fragile-X syndrome evaluation

TEST PERFORMED
FRAXA Expansion Mutation Analysis
Gene: FMR1 (Fragile X Mental Retardation 1)
Methodology: PCR-based sizing assay for CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene

METHODOLOGY
Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood. PCR amplification was performed using fluorescently labeled primers flanking the CGG repeat region in the 5' UTR of the FMR1 gene. Fragment analysis was performed by capillary electrophoresis with internal size standards. This assay detects normal, intermediate, premutation, and full mutation alleles in the FRAXA locus.

Detection Limitations:
- Lower limit of detection: 5 CGG repeats
- Upper limit of reliable detection: ~200 CGG repeats
- Full mutations (>200 repeats) may appear as absent amplification
- This assay does not detect point mutations, deletions, or other rearrangements in FMR1

RESULTS
FMR1 CGG Repeat Analysis:
Allele 1: 31 (±1) CGG repeats - NORMAL
Allele 2: Not detected (consistent with single allele in males or homozygous females)

Interpretation: Normal allele detected

Reference Ranges:
Normal: 6-45 CGG repeats
Intermediate: 46-54 CGG repeats
Premutation: 55-200 CGG repeats
Full mutation: >200 CGG repeats

SUMMARY
Molecular testing for FRAXA expansion in the FMR1 gene reveals a normal allele with 31 (±1) CGG repeats. No expansion allele is present. These results indicate that the patient is very unlikely to have Fragile-X syndrome.

It should be noted that rare cases of Fragile-X syndrome (<1%) may result from point mutations or genomic rearrangements within the FMR1 gene that are not detected by this PCR-based repeat expansion assay. If clinical suspicion remains high, additional testing methods such as FMR1 sequencing or deletion/duplication analysis may be considered.

This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by [redacted location] Medical Center Molecular Genetics Laboratory. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
